steps.body: A fraction can share a SET as well as a shape: 12 counters split into 3 equal groups makes each group one-third of the set.
steps.narration: A fraction can share a SET as well as a shape: 12 counters split into 3 equal groups makes each group one-third of the set.

widget.prompt: A set of 8 counters is split into 4 equal groups. Build the fraction one group represents.
widget.successFeedback: 1/4 — four equal groups, and one of them is a fourth of the whole set.
widget.lowFeedback: Your shaded bar is shorter than the target half. Shade more — raise the numerator, or use fewer parts.
widget.highFeedback: Your shaded bar is longer than half. Shade less — lower the numerator, or split into more parts.

commonFractions.feedback: 1/8 would name one COUNTER out of eight, not one of the four equal groups.
4/4 is the entire set — all four groups together.

predict.prompt: 12 counters in 3 equal groups. What fraction of the set is one group?
predict.reveal: There are three equal groups, so each is one third — even though each holds four counters.

cml.actionGoal: Cut, count, and compare equal pieces to see what g3f set model really names.
invariants: A fraction names equal shares of ONE whole: the denominator says how many equal pieces the whole became, and the numerator counts them, which is what makes g3f set model comparable at all.
misconceptions: Calling unequal pieces fractions, reading the denominator as a count, or comparing fractions that came from different-sized wholes.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If the whole changed size, which of these comparisons would stop being trustworthy?

widget.prompt: A set is arranged in 5 rows of 3 counters. How many counters in the whole set?

commonErrors.feedback: That added the rows to the columns; a grid holds rows GROUPS of 3.
That is one row short — count every row, including the last.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Name the equal pieces the whole was cut into, then count how many of them the question is about.

widget.prompt: Which is bigger: a third or a fourth?

options.label: a third
options.feedback: Correct — more pieces in the same whole means each piece is smaller, so a third wins "bigger".

options.label: a fourth
options.feedback: a fourth is not the bigger one — compare how many pieces the whole was cut into.

options.label: they're the same size
options.feedback: They differ: the same whole cut into more pieces gives smaller pieces every time.

widget.prompt: A ribbon is cut into 6 equal pieces and 5 are used. Which fraction names what was used?

options.label: 5/6 — five of six equal pieces
options.feedback: Correct — the denominator counts the equal pieces the whole became, and the numerator counts the ones used.

options.label: 6/5 — six pieces, five used
options.feedback: That puts the whole on top; the piece count belongs underneath, and 6/5 would be more than one ribbon.

options.label: 1/6 — one piece was used
options.feedback: 1/6 names a single piece, but five of them were used, not one.

options.label: 1/5 — five pieces
options.feedback: The ribbon was cut into SIX pieces, so sixths are the piece size no matter how many were used.
